glossary.short: a statement you say is true and can defend with evidence
a system that contains two or more independently managed elements
one of the independently managed systems inside a system of systems

each constituent's owner keeps the authority to decide about it
the policies and decision structures that constrain the managers of the constituents

transfer.title: Transfer case · the textbook's iLearn digital learning environment
transfer.text: The textbook's iLearn system is a national initiative for schools. To create a digital learning environment, it must integrate with each local authority's network management and school administration systems. There is no common governance process across the authorities. This is a different system from the incident dashboard.
transfer.source: Source slide 19 (iLearn as a system of systems)
transfer.question: Which class of system of systems is iLearn, and why?
transfer.answer: A coalition, Maier's virtual class. No formal governance body spans the authorities. Each manages its own systems and collaborates informally. Its technical complexity is modest, but its governance complexity is high.
transfer.concept: classifying a system of systems by governance
transfer.answerKey: a coalition, because no shared governance exists

X01.commonError: Students judge a system of systems by code size. Ask who can change each part without asking anyone else.
bullets: Operational independence: constituents remain useful as systems in their own right.
Managerial independence: constituent owners retain decision authority.
Independent changes and interactions affect shared behavior.
Geographic distribution, heterogeneity and large data volumes.

X02.answerKey: a governance constraint, not a defect
X02.commonError: Students file every obstacle under technical complexity. Ask whether a better design could remove it; if not, it is managerial or governance.

X02A.commonError: Students classify by network links. Classify by authority: who can set priorities and resolve disputes.
X02A.answerKey2: federated: a joint body whose decisions owners implement
X02A.question2: Which classification fits an agreed joint governing body whose decisions participants implement?
X02A.answer2: The author's federated system of systems, Maier's collaborative category. A coalition without that formal body is different.

lists.title: Maier's classification
items: Directed: owned by a single organisation and built from systems that organisation also owns; parts may be independently managed
Collaborative: no central authority sets priorities or resolves disputes; elements are owned by different organisations
Virtual: no central governance; participants may not agree on the purpose and may enter or leave

lists.title: More intuitive terms
items: Organizational: governance and management lie within one organisation
Federated: governance depends on a voluntary body in which all owners are represented
Coalition: no formal governance; organisations collaborate informally and manage their own systems

X03.commonError: Students trust a correct interface specification as a guarantee. Ask who can change the meaning behind it without telling anyone.

CHECK1.answerKey: its own display, validation and fallback
CHECK1.commonError: Students promise on behalf of the providers. Separate what the dashboard controls from what it only receives.
CHECK1.answer: Not without the corresponding authority, agreement and evidence. It can promise its own display, validation and fallback behaviour, with limits.

X04.answerKey: authority and acceptance decide what is feasible
X04.commonError: Students leave governance to the end. Agreements on authority and change can take longer than the interface itself.
X04.answer: Authority, participation, change handling and acceptance decide which integrations are feasible. They can take longer to agree than an interface takes to implement.

X05.answerKey: different workflows can make unification costly
X05.commonError: Students assume one unified interface is always better. Ask whose daily workflow it slows down.

DEPLOY.answerKey: a defined capability with acceptance evidence
DEPLOY.commonError: Students describe a stage as “the parts done so far”. Ask what useful work it does and how acceptance is shown.
bullets: An incomplete SoS should still perform useful, limited work.
Constituents may already be deployed and cannot all be frozen.
Add a coherent capability with explicit acceptance conditions.
Plan training, equipment and operational transition as well as code.

X06.answerKey: record participant versions, inputs and assumptions
X06.commonError: Students record only the result. Ask which participant versions and data assumptions the result depended on.

CHECK2.answerKey: old data shown as current hides uncertainty
CHECK2.commonError: Students show the last values to keep the screen full. Ask what a user would do differently if they saw “unavailable”.
CHECK2.answer: It presents unsupported certainty. A service with limits must preserve freshness and uncertainty information so users can interpret the result.

X09.answerKey: the capability depends on continued participation
X09.commonError: Students treat an architecture framework as a solution. It offers views and a checklist; it cannot create authority.
X09.answerKey2: a checklist and vocabulary, not authority
X09.question: Why is an incentive to maintain a data feed an architectural concern?
X09.answer: The capability depends on continued participation. An elegant interface cannot sustain the service when an independent owner has no reason to maintain it.
X09.question2: When can a framework remain useful despite its limitations?
X09.answer2: As a checklist and shared vocabulary for architectural concerns. The team must not assume it solves independent ownership or uncertain boundaries.
X09.extra: The chapter's seven principles are Maier's four and Sillitto's three. Deliver value when incomplete. Be realistic about control. Focus on interfaces. Provide collaboration incentives. Design as nodes and a web. Specify behaviour as services exchanged between nodes. Understand and manage vulnerabilities.

lists.title: General principles for architecting a system of systems
items: Design systems so that they can deliver value if they are incomplete
Be realistic about what can be controlled
Focus on the system interfaces
Provide collaboration incentives
Design a system of systems as a node and web architecture
Specify behaviour as services exchanged between nodes
Understand and manage system vulnerabilities

X08.answerKey: no unbounded wait and no misleading substitute value
X08.commonError: Students let one slow feed delay the whole display. Define the timeout and what the missing cell shows.

lists.title: Systems as data feeds
items: A principal system requires data of different types
The data is available from other systems, which the principal system queries
The systems that provide data generally do not interact with each other
Often seen in organizational or federated systems where some governance exists

CONTAINER.answerKey: a link does not give common sign-in or storage
CONTAINER.commonError: Students think adding a tool to the menu integrates it. Each approved system needs its own interface to the common services.

TRADING.answerKey: no principal system; participants exchange directly
TRADING.commonError: Students describe trading as a two-way data feed. The difference is the missing principal system and the missing governance.
TRADING.answer: In a trading system of systems there is no principal system. Participants exchange information with one another, one-to-one or one-to-many. Each publishes its own interface. In the data-feed pattern, a principal system queries providers that do not interact with each other.

AISYS.concept: promising about another owner's AI feed
AISYS.answerKey: show source, timestamp and model version; label the rest unverified
AISYS.commonError: Students promise that the classifications are correct. The dashboard cannot inspect or version the agency's model.
AISYS.answer: Not that the classifications are correct. The dashboard cannot inspect or version the model. It can promise to show each item with its source, timestamp and the producer's declared model version. It can flag detected shifts, such as a sudden change in the share of high-severity incidents. It can label affected data as unverified. It can seek an agreement that participants announce model changes as interface changes, with a trial period. The promise is limited to what the dashboard observes. Governance covers the rest.

APPLY.answerKey: label freshness and model version; mark changed data unverified
APPLY.commonError: Students fix the schedule and miss the model change. Same interface shape does not mean the same meaning.
APPLY.answer: A defensible revision responds to the changed assumption, keeps missing evidence visible and names a responsible role. For the AI-produced feed, show its declared model version. Flag data produced since the change as unverified until the agency confirms how its classifications changed.
APPLY.sourceLabel: Course addition · not from the textbook · applies the chapter to the case

stations.answerKey: source, timestamp and declared model version, not correctness
stations.think: Devices down. What useful service can be promised without pretending to control every owner?
stations.pair: Name one assumption and one given fact you need to support your answer.
stations.write: Write your claim and its evidence. Mark any test you only propose as proposed.
stations.hint: Name the service or property first. Use a source definition and the given facts. Ask which missing fact would change your claim. Decide what can be promised about a feed produced by another owner's AI model.
stations.note: Think without devices, then pair. Choosing when not to use technology is part of using it well. Use the same card; nobody is marked on field length or a timer.
stations.answer: An answer with limits separates the given facts from the needed evidence. A source explanation supports a mechanism. It does not prove the fictional deployment passed a test. The dashboard can promise what it observes: source, timestamp and declared model version. It cannot promise the correctness of classifications made by a model it cannot inspect.

criteria.name: Names the mechanism
levels: Names the chapter mechanism that decides the case and says how it applies.
Names a mechanism but does not connect it to the case facts.
No chapter mechanism, or the wrong one.

criteria.name: Uses only the given facts
levels: Every statement rests on a given fact or is marked as an assumption.
Mostly given facts, but one invented or unmarked assumption.
Relies on facts the case does not give.

criteria.name: Evidence another person can check
levels: Names evidence a second engineer could inspect, and marks proposed tests as proposed.
Names evidence, but it is vague or its status is unclear.
Opinion or confidence instead of evidence.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: Claim: the dashboard shows each item with its source and timestamp and marks any feed older than its agreed interval. Given: it validates and displays; it cannot set update schedules. Proposed: a staleness check per feed. Nothing is promised about the agency's model.
strong.why: Names the mechanism (managerial independence), keeps to the given facts and proposes a checkable test.

weak.text: The dashboard guarantees all incidents are current and correctly classified.
weak.why: Promises what other owners control; no evidence.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.answerKey: monitoring can flag a shift but not prove which classification is right
stations.think: Compare two mechanisms: validating feed shape only, or also monitoring each feed's content for sudden shifts and labelling it. Which one would you choose?
stations.pair: Ask your partner to argue for the mechanism you rejected. Name one trade-off and one thing both mechanisms share.
stations.write: Write why your mechanism supports your claim, and what you are still unsure of.
stations.hint: Explain why the mechanism affects your claim. Then name a shared cause, a mismatch or a limit outside its evidence.
stations.answer: Tie the chosen mechanism to the required property. Say what the alternative improves or sacrifices. Evidence of a shared dependency or mismatched assumption can defeat an apparently stronger design. Shape validation cannot see a change in meaning. Monitoring distributions, for example the share of high-severity incidents, can flag a shift. It cannot prove which classification is right.

criteria.name: Links the mechanism to the property
levels: Explains how the chosen mechanism affects the property at stake.
Names the mechanism without the link to the property.

criteria.name: Names a shared cause or limit
levels: Names a specific shared cause, mismatch or limit that could defeat the mechanism.
Mentions a limit in general terms only.
Treats the mechanism as always enough.

criteria.name: States the trade-off
levels: Says what the alternative improves and what it costs.
Gives one side of the trade-off only.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: Shape validation plus content monitoring, because the property is honest display and a model change alters meaning without altering shape. Its limit: a flagged shift shows that something changed, not which classification is right. It costs a baseline per feed.
strong.why: Links the mechanism to the property, names the limit and states the cost.

weak.text: Shape validation is enough; if the schema passes, the data is fine.
weak.why: Equates schema with meaning; no limit, no trade-off.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.answerKey: label what the dashboard cannot vouch for and agree how model changes are announced
stations.think: One feed moves to a slower update schedule while keeping the same interface shape. The same agency also changed its AI model version. The shape is unchanged, but incidents are now classified differently. Does your first decision still hold?
stations.pair: Explain what changes in your claim, your evidence or its scope.
stations.write: Record the new evidence and your revised decision with its limits. Say plainly what your first card got wrong. Name the responsible role and who must be told.
stations.hint: Do not simply repeat your first answer. Name the changed assumption, the next evidence and the condition that would change your decision.
stations.note: Classroom version only. The assessed assignment has its own new evidence, revealed after you commit.
stations.answer: The new fact changes the stated assumption, so the original evidence cannot be widened silently. Retain, restrict or revise the decision with a reason, a new verification requirement and a named owner. Freshness and meaning both changed with no schema change. The dashboard must label what it cannot vouch for. It must agree with the agency how model changes are announced.

criteria.name: Says what the new fact changes
levels: Names the assumption the new fact breaks and what it leaves intact.
Notes the new fact without saying which assumption it breaks.
Ignores or restates the new fact.

criteria.name: Revises with a reason
levels: Keeps, changes or replaces the decision for a reason from the new fact. Says what the first answer got wrong.
Changes the decision without a clear reason, or hides the first answer.

criteria.name: Names the owner and who is told
levels: Names the role that decides and the people who must be informed.
Names neither the owner nor who is told.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: My first card assumed an unchanged shape meant unchanged meaning; it did not. Revise: show model version and freshness per feed, mark data since the change as unverified, and seek an announcement agreement. The dashboard owner decides; the agencies and the public are told.
strong.why: Names the broken assumption, revises with a reason, admits the first error, names owner and audience.

weak.text: Keep my promise as it is; the schema still validates.
weak.why: Ignores the meaning change; names nobody.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

quiz.concept: definition of a system of systems
quiz.answerKey: two or more independently managed elements

quiz.why: Federated systems depend on a voluntary governance body of all owners. Coalitions have no formal governance. Organizational systems of systems are governed within one organisation.
Reductionism assumes a single controlling authority, rational technical decisions and clear boundaries. A system of systems has several owners, and decisions are often political.
There may be no detailed specification. Constituents may change during testing. Problems may need intermediate software rather than changes to a constituent.

quiz.answerKey: trading systems have no principal system
quiz.why: In a trading system of systems, processing can happen in any system and participants exchange information directly. Data feeds and containers both have a principal system.

48.reason: Definition of an architectural pattern; in the study list

items: A principal system requires data of different types
The principal system queries other systems to get the data
The providing systems generally do not interact with each other
Often observed in organizational or federated systems with some governance
The ‘systems as data feeds’ architecture is an appropriate architecture to use when it is possible to identify entities in a unique way and create relatively simple queries about these entities.
A variant of the ‘systems as data feeds’ architecture arises when there are a number of systems involved which provide similar data but which are not identical.
The architecture has to include an intermediate layer to translate the general query from the principal system into the specific query required by the individual information system.
Systems in a container are systems of systems where one of the systems acts as a virtual container and provides a set of common services such as an authentication and a storage service.
Conceptually, other systems are then placed into this container to make their functionality accessible to system users.

You don’t place systems into a real container to implement these systems of systems. Rather, for each approved system, there is a separate interface that allows it to be integrated with the common services.

aiAssignment.scenario: A city dashboard coordinates ambulances from three independent owners: two public hospitals and a private ambulance company. Each owner runs its own AI system to rank incoming calls by urgency. Each publishes its ranked queue to the dashboard.

criteria.name: FIT
levels: Names the chapter concept that decides the case and shows why it fits these facts.
Names the right concept, with only a partial link to the facts.
Names a concept but does not connect it to the case.
No chapter concept, or the wrong one.

criteria.name: BOUND
levels: States an observable condition that would end the claim.
Names a condition, but nobody could easily observe it.
Gives a vague limit, such as “if it fails”.

criteria.name: ACT + EVIDENCE
levels: One concrete action with an owner, and evidence another engineer could inspect even if the AI is wrong.
A concrete action, but the evidence is weak or its status is unclear.
General advice, or evidence that relies on the AI's own output.

criteria.name: REFIT
levels: Uses the new information, names the assumption it broke and justifies retain, revise or replace.
Uses the new information but does not name the broken assumption.
Keeps or changes the answer without a reason.

criteria.name: OWNER + AI USE
levels: Names the role that accepts the risk and who must be told. Declares any AI help and how it was checked.
Names a role, but not who must be told, or the AI declaration is incomplete.
Names “the team” or “the system” as owner.
No owner and no AI declaration.

rubric.marks: Practice only · not graded · score yourself 1, 0.75, 0.5 or 0 per criterion

strong.text: The dashboard can promise only what it observes: each owner's queue, its time and its declared model version. It must not merge the rankings. The promise ends if one owner's share of urgent calls shifts without notice. Action: the city lead seeks an agreement to announce model changes. Evidence: a per-owner baseline with a drift alert, proposed. After the weighting change I replace the merged list with per-owner queues.
strong.why: Separates what the dashboard controls from what it receives, names an observable limit, an owner and evidence, and revises.

weak.text: The dashboard is in charge, so it sorts all calls by urgency score.
weak.why: Assumes scores mean the same across owners and that display gives authority.

rubric.other: they use a chapter concept, rest on the given facts and name evidence someone else can check. A different verdict that meets these conditions is as strong as the strong example.

criteria.name: FIT
criteria.strong: The concept is managerial independence: three owners, three models, one interface. Given: the dashboard can read but not change any model; no agreement on announcing changes. Assumption, marked: the owners rank by the same idea of urgency.
criteria.strongWhy: Names the chapter concept, keeps to the given facts and marks the assumption.
criteria.weak: The dashboard is in charge because it shows everything.
criteria.weakWhy: Confuses display with authority; no case fact.

criteria.name: INTEGRATE
criteria.strong: Treat each queue as a data feed. Show each call with its owner, timestamp and the owner's declared model version. Never merge the three rankings into one city-wide order without an agreed scale.
criteria.strongWhy: Applies the data-feed pattern and keeps the owners' meanings separate.
criteria.weak: Merge the three queues and sort by urgency score.
criteria.weakWhy: Assumes the scores mean the same thing across owners.

criteria.name: BOUND
criteria.strong: The promise holds while each owner's ranking rule and model version are unchanged and declared. An undeclared change in the share of high-urgency calls from one owner reopens it.
criteria.strongWhy: Names the dependency and an observable trigger.
criteria.weak: It works as long as everyone is honest.
criteria.weakWhy: No dependency and no observable trigger.

criteria.name: ACT + EVIDENCE
criteria.strong: Action: an agreement that model changes are announced as interface changes with a trial period, owned by the city dispatch lead. Evidence: a per-owner baseline of urgency shares with a drift alert, proposed.
criteria.strongWhy: Feasible action, a named role, evidence with its status.
criteria.weak: Ask the owners to be careful.
criteria.weakWhy: No specific action, owner or inspectable evidence.

criteria.name: REFIT
criteria.strong: The private company's weighting shows my merged view was promising a fairness it could not check. I replace it: rankings are shown per owner with the model version, and the drift alert fires. My first plan assumed one shared idea of urgency.
criteria.strongWhy: Names what changed, chooses REPLACE with a reason, admits the first assumption.
criteria.weak: I keep the merged list; the dashboard cannot control the owners anyway.
criteria.weakWhy: Uses lack of control as an excuse; ignores the given fact.

assignmentRubric.other: the answer names the chapter concept that decides, uses only the facts given in the task, separates what the dashboard controls from what it receives, and names evidence from a baseline or record that someone else can check. A different integration that meets these conditions earns the same marks as the model answer.
